chunks: Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub and Hammad ibn Isa and Safwan ibn Yahya, from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)
About a woman who runs between al-Safa and al-Marwah on a beast or on a camel, he said: 'There is no harm in that.' And I asked him about a man who does that, and he said: 'There is no harm.'

key_terms.السَّعْي: The ritual running/walking between Safa and Marwah
key_terms.الصَّفَا: Al-Safa, one of the two hills in Mecca
key_terms.دَابَّة: Beast of burden (animal used for riding)
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: There is no harm / It is permissible
key_terms.وَالْمَرْوَة: Al-Marwah, the second hill in Mecca

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to ride a camel or horse while performing Sa'i between Safa and Marwah?
ai.summary: Reported by Shaykh al-Tusi in *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, this hadith clarifies the flexibility of the Sa'i ritual by confirming that riding a beast of burden is permissible (la ba'sa) for both men and women. This ruling reflects the Shia juristic principle of removing hardship (raf' al-haraj), allowing pilgrims to fulfill the obligation of traversing between Safa and Marwah without the physical strain of walking, provided the movement is maintained. It underscores the practical adaptability of ritual acts in Shia fiqh while preserving their essential spiritual intent.
